Hands-on Exercise 7a: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R

Author

Lei Yuhe

Published

May 14, 2026

Modified

July 3, 2026

1 Overview

This chapter covers how to model, analyse and visualise network data using R.

Objectives:

  • create graph object data frames and manipulate them with dplyr, lubridate, and tidygraph
  • build network graph visualisations with ggraph
  • compute network metrics (centrality, community) with tidygraph
  • build advanced graph visualisations that incorporate these metrics
  • build interactive network visualisations with visNetwork

Source data: an oil exploration/extraction company’s internal email network (the GAStech case data), consisting of an edges file (who emailed whom) and a nodes file (employee attributes).

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and launching R packages

Packages needed for this chapter:

Package Purpose
igraph Core network data structures & algorithms
tidygraph Tidy (dplyr-style) API for graph manipulation
ggraph ggplot2-style grammar for network graphs
visNetwork Interactive network graphs (vis.js)
tidyverse Data wrangling
lubridate Date/time handling
clock Additional date/time utilities
graphlayouts Extra layout algorithms for ggraph
concaveman Concave hulls (used with ggforce)
ggforce Extra ggplot2 geoms, e.g. geom_mark_hull()
Code 
pacman::p_load(igraph, tidygraph, ggraph,
                visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
                tidyverse, graphlayouts,
                concaveman, ggforce)

2.2 Importing network data from files

Code 
GAStech_nodes <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_node.csv")
GAStech_edges <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv")

SentDate is imported as character, not date. This needs to be fixed before any time-based analysis or visualisation can be done.

2.4 Wrangling time

Code 
GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SentDate,
                         label = TRUE,
                         abbr = FALSE))

Notes to self:

  • dmy() and wday() are both lubridate functions.
  • dmy() parses a day-month-year character string into a proper Date.
  • wday() extracts the weekday; label = TRUE returns names instead of numbers, and abbr = FALSE keeps full names (e.g. “Monday” not “Mon”).
  • The resulting Weekday column is an ordinal (ordered factor) field.

2.5 Reviewing the revised date fields

2.6 Wrangling attributes

Raw edges are individual email records, which is too granular for a clear network plot. Aggregate by sender, receiver, and weekday to get an edge weight (count of emails):

Code 
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

Notes to self:

  • Four dplyr verbs at work: filter(), group_by(), summarise(), ungroup().
  • filter(source != target) removes self-loops (emails to oneself).
  • filter(Weight > 1) drops very weak (one-off) ties to reduce clutter.
  • Output: 1,372 rows, a much more usable edge list.

glimpse(GAStech_edges_aggregated)

3 Creating Network Objects Using tidygraph

tidygraph gives a tidy API for graph manipulation. A network isn’t naturally “tidy,” but it can be represented as two tidy tables (nodes + edges), and tidygraph provides a clean way to move between them.

Recommended background reading:

  • Introducing tidygraph
  • tidygraph 1.1 — A tidy hope

3.1 The tbl_graph object

Two constructors:

  • tbl_graph() build a tbl_graph directly from separate nodes and edges data frames.
  • as_tbl_graph() convert an existing network object/data structure into a tbl_graph. Supported inputs include: node/edge data frame pairs, base R data.frame/list/matrix, igraph objects, network objects, dendrogram/hclust, data.tree::Node, ape::phylo/evonet, and Bioconductor graphNEL/graphAM/graphBAM objects.

3.2 The dplyr verbs in tidygraph

  • activate() switches which internal tibble (nodes or edges) is “active.” Any dplyr verb applied to a tbl_graph acts on whichever tibble is currently active.
  • While manipulating one tibble, you can still reach into the other:
    • .N() access the node data
    • .E() access the edge data
    • .G() access the whole tbl_graph object

3.3 Using tbl_graph() to build the tidygraph data model

Code 
GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = GAStech_nodes,
                            edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated,
                            directed = TRUE)

4 Plotting Static Network Graphs with ggraph

ggraph extends ggplot2’s grammar of graphics to networks. Three core building blocks:

  • nodes
  • edges
  • layouts

4.1 Plotting a basic network graph

Code 
ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()

Notes to self: ggraph() accepts either an igraph or a tbl_graph object, plus a layout argument (defaults to "nicely" if unspecified).

4.2 Changing the default network graph theme

Code 
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()

theme_graph() strips axes/grid/border and swaps in a network-friendly default font (Arial Narrow, overridable). Can be applied per-plot with theme_graph() or globally with set_graph_style().

4.3 Changing the coloring of the plot

Code 
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = 'grey50')) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = 'grey40'))

g + theme_graph(background = 'grey10',
                text_colour = 'white')

4.4 Working with ggraph’s layouts

Supported standard layouts: star, circle, nicely (default), dh, gem, graphopt, grid, mds, sphere, randomly, fr, kk, drl, lgl.

4.5 Fruchterman and Reingold layout

Code 
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()

layout = "fr" selects the Fruchterman–Reingold force-directed layout.

4.6 Modifying network nodes

Colour nodes by Department:

Code 
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = 3))

g + theme_graph()

geom_node_point() is the network analogue of geom_point() — supports colour, size, shape aesthetics just like ggplot2.

4.7 Modifying edges

Map edge thickness to Weight:

Code 
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 3)

g + theme_graph()

width maps line thickness proportionally to Weight; alpha adds transparency to reduce over-plotting.

5 Creating Facet Graphs

Faceting spreads nodes/edges across panels by attribute value, reducing edge over-plotting. Three ggraph faceting functions:

  • facet_nodes() - an edge is drawn in a panel only if both its terminal nodes are present in that panel.
  • facet_edges() - nodes are drawn in every panel, regardless of the faceting variable.
  • facet_graph() - facet on two variables simultaneously.

5.1 Working with facet_edges()

Code 
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)

5.2 Repositioning the legend

Code 
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)

5.3 A framed facet graph

Code 
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

5.4 Working with facet_nodes()

Code 
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_nodes(~Department) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

6 Network Metrics Analysis

6.1 Computing centrality indices

Centrality measures describe how “important” an actor is within a network. Four classic measures: degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector.

Note

For the underlying theory/maths, see Chapter 7: Actor Prominence in A User’s Guide to Network Analysis in R.

Code 
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                       size = betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()

mutate() (dplyr) + centrality_betweenness() (tidygraph) computes and stores betweenness centrality as a new node attribute.

6.2 Visualising network metrics

From ggraph v2.0 onward, tidygraph algorithms (like centrality functions) can be called directly inside a ggraph aes() mapping, no need to precompute and store them first:

Code 
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                       size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()

6.3 Visualising community

tidygraph exposes many igraph community-detection algorithms:

  • Edge-betweenness - group_edge_betweenness()
  • Leading eigenvector — group_leading_eigen()
  • Fast-greedy — group_fast_greedy()
  • Louvain — group_louvain()
  • Walktrap — group_walktrap()
  • Label propagation — group_label_prop()
  • InfoMAP — group_infomap()
  • Spinglass — group_spinglass()
  • Optimal — group_optimal()

Some account for edge direction/weight, some don’t — see the tidygraph community reference.

Code 
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = Weight),
    alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()

6.3.1 Adding hulls around communities

Uses geom_mark_hull() from ggforce (requires ggforce + concaveman) to visually enclose each detected community:

Code 
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y,
        group = community,
        fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),   # how far the hull extends beyond points
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")   # corner smoothness
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight),
                 alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                       size = betweenness_measure),
                  color = "black",
                  shape = 21)

g + theme_graph()

7 Building Interactive Network Graphs with visNetwork

visNetwork wraps the vis.js JavaScript library for interactive network visualisation.

Key requirements:

  • The nodes list must include an id column.
  • The edges list must have from and to columns.
  • Node labels are drawn from the nodes list’s label column.
  • Interactive features: drag nodes (auto re-spacing), zoom, and pan.

7.1 Data preparation

Code 
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
  summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

7.2 Plotting the first interactive network graph

Code 
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated)

7.3 Working with layout

Code 
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")

See visIgraphLayout docs for available layout options.

7.4 Working with visual attributes — Nodes

visNetwork() colours nodes by a field named group, so rename Department to group:

Code 
GAStech_nodes <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)
Code 
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

7.5 Working with visual attributes — Edges

visEdges() controls edge appearance:

  • arrows — where to place arrowheads (e.g. "to")
  • smooth — draw edges as smooth/curved lines
Code 
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(enabled = TRUE,
                         type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

See visEdges options for more.

7.6 Interactivity

visOptions() adds interactive behaviours:

  • highlightNearest = TRUE — highlight a node’s neighbours on click
  • nodesIdSelection = TRUE — adds an HTML dropdown to jump to a node by id
Code 
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE,
             nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

See visOptions for the full argument list.

8 Key Takeaways

  1. Two-table model: every network = one nodes table + one edges table; tidygraph::tbl_graph() binds them into one object.
  2. activate() decides which table (nodes/edges) your dplyr verbs act on — a very easy thing to forget mid-pipeline.
  3. ggraph = ggplot2 for networks: same aes()/geom logic, with network-specific geoms (geom_node_point(), geom_edge_link()) and layouts (fr, kk, nicely, etc.).
  4. Faceting (facet_edges(), facet_nodes()) is a powerful way to reduce over-plotting by splitting the network across a categorical or temporal variable.
  5. Centrality & community detection can be computed inline inside a ggraph() call (v2.0+) — no separate mutate() step required.
  6. visNetwork trades static ggraph plots for browser-based interactivity (pan/zoom/drag/highlight), useful for exploratory analysis or dashboards.
